title: Alternative protein in Vietnam: a supply-side scoping study

pages.title: Alternative protein in Vietnam: a supply-side scoping study
pages.summary: A draft, evidence-tagged scoping study of what alternative protein Vietnam could make for people to eat, and of the demand that would pull it, with feed only as context. Written for investors, policy makers, startups, manufacturers, research bodies and international organisations.

pages.title: The report in two minutes
pages.summary: The whole report on one screen: why Vietnam, what the food-security evidence does and does not support, what it could make for people to eat, who would buy it, what stands in the way, what to do first and what 2050 looks like.

pages.title: Executive summary
pages.summary: Vietnam's case for making more protein for people at home is a security case, real but narrow: about two thirds of the animal protein people eat rests on imports, directly or through feed, and only protein made from domestic inputs reduces that. The first openings are domestic textured plant protein, a cassava-starch-to-fermentation-sugar hub and shared pilot fermentation; firms, not shoppers, would buy new protein as an ingredient; and the main public lever is a new-food clause in the Food Safety Law.

pages.title: Tóm tắt báo cáo
pages.summary: Lý do để Việt Nam tự làm thêm protein cho người dân ăn là lý do an ninh, có cơ sở nhưng hẹp: khoảng hai phần ba lượng đạm động vật người dân ăn dựa vào nhập khẩu, trực tiếp hoặc qua thức ăn chăn nuôi, và chỉ protein làm từ nguyên liệu trong nước mới giảm được tỷ lệ đó. Cơ hội đầu tiên là đạm thực vật tạo cấu trúc sản xuất trong nước, một cụm nhà máy chuyển tinh bột sắn thành đường lên men, và lên men thử nghiệm dùng chung. Người mua protein mới là doanh nghiệp, mua làm nguyên liệu, chứ không phải người mua lẻ. Công cụ chính của Nhà nước là một điều khoản về thực phẩm mới trong Luật An toàn thực phẩm.

pages.title: At a glance
pages.summary: The numbers that frame protein for people in Vietnam, where it comes from, supply and demand, today and to 2050, on one page, with links to the chapters behind them. Feed numbers appear only as context.

pages.title: Prologue: alternative protein for newcomers
pages.summary: For readers new to the field: what alternative protein is, the main families of technology and how each is made, the general arguments for and against it, where the world stands in 2026 on markets, money and rules, where Vietnam fits and why this study is about protein for people, and the terms and conventions needed to read the report.

pages.title: Lời mở đầu: protein thay thế cho người mới tìm hiểu
pages.summary: Dành cho người mới: protein thay thế là gì, các nhóm công nghệ chính và cách làm ra từng loại, những lập luận ủng hộ và phản đối, bức tranh thế giới năm 2026 về thị trường, dòng vốn và quy định, vị trí của Việt Nam và vì sao nghiên cứu này bàn về protein cho con người, cùng các thuật ngữ và quy ước cần biết để đọc báo cáo.

pages.title: How to read this report
pages.summary: What the report covers (protein for people, with feed only as context), how it is organised, which pages to read for which purpose, what the tags, codes and scenario names mean, and the conventions for numbers, names and corrections.

pages.title: Frequently asked questions
pages.summary: Short answers to the questions people ask most about this draft report, its scope (protein for people), alternative protein, Vietnam's prospects and food security, and using the report and its data, with links to the pages that give the full answer.

pages.title: Why Vietnam: the protein people eat, and the imports behind it
pages.part: I. Context
pages.summary: Vietnamese people eat more meat each year. About one fifth of their protein is imported food, and about two thirds of the animal protein rests on imports, directly or through the feed behind domestic meat, eggs and fish. Imported meat and dairy are a second, smaller exposure, driven by lower costs abroad rather than subsidies. The import exposure, with industrial value and trade, is the strongest case for making more protein for people at home. But only protein made from domestic inputs reduces it, and at the scale demand supports, new protein adds a second source rather than cutting the exposure.

pages.title: The alternative-protein economy today
pages.part: I. Context
pages.summary: Vietnam's real non-animal protein economy is incumbent: soy milk, tofu and industrial đồ chay made by meat and frozen-food processors. Most of it is low in protein, and every locally made high-protein product runs on imported textured soy or wheat gluten, much of it from China. Modern plant-based brands are nearly absent, and we found no Vietnamese maker of fermented protein ingredients for food.

pages.title: Vietnam in the region
pages.part: I. Context
pages.summary: Vietnam ranks near the top in Asia on production cost and at the bottom on rules. Singapore approves, Thailand and Korea have routes but few approvals, and China builds at scale. Vietnam already supplies the region's bio-industries with cassava starch, but the starch it exports is turned into fermentation sugar in China. The regional lesson is that a published procedure with a fixed timeline matters more than cheap labour.

pages.title: What Vietnam has: raw materials and side streams
pages.part: II. Supply: what Vietnam can make
pages.summary: Vietnam is rich in fermentable carbohydrate (cassava, rice, sugar) and poor in protein-rich side streams. For protein for people, the carbohydrate is clean carbon for food fermentation, and small food-grade side streams such as okara and brewer's grain suit koji and fungal foods. The carbohydrate is mostly already traded, often to China, and nobody measures the residues.

pages.title: The industrial base: fermentation and food processing
pages.part: II. Supply: what Vietnam can make
pages.summary: Vietnam has large, modern food, brewing and fermentation industries, but its aerobic fermentation capacity is captive inside three amino-acid makers. There is no food-grade contract fermentation, open pilot plant, protein-isolate plant or domestic textured-protein extruder. A new food-protein venture can use frozen-food co-packers, cassava glucose and trained staff, but has to bring its own process equipment or negotiate with an incumbent.

pages.title: Knowledge, talent and shared infrastructure
pages.part: II. Supply: what Vietnam can make
pages.summary: Vietnam's research base sits next to alternative protein rather than inside it: strong in aquafeed trials, yeast protein expression, stem-cell culture, koji genetics and microalgae; near zero in texturisation, mycoprotein, precision fermentation and food cell lines. Its novel-food research intensity is about a quarter to a third of Thailand's. For protein for people, the binding gap is shared infrastructure: no open pilot fermentation, no food extrusion line and no protein-digestibility testing.

pages.title: Rules of the game: routes to market, incentives and reforms
pages.part: II. Supply: what Vietnam can make
pages.summary: Vietnam has no novel-food gate: new protein foods enter through self-declaration, under legal uncertainty and with no way to get an ingredient positively cleared, and precision-fermented proteins probably count as GMO products. The new Food Safety Law, due for first comments in October 2026 and considered for passage in May 2027, is a one-off window to add a proportionate new-food procedure. Feed rules appear only as context.

pages.title: Capital
pages.part: II. Supply: what Vietnam can make
pages.summary: Only one alternative-protein deal in Vietnam has exceeded USD 5 million: Entobel's insect-meal plant. It is an insect-feed deal outside this study's focus, but its structure (local private equity, a small development-finance ticket and a seafood exporter's offtake) is the one proven template. Agriculture venture capital in Vietnam was about USD 1 million in 2025, new state venture funds are small, and global alternative-protein investment has shifted towards fermentation and ingredients.

pages.title: Economics: what it costs and what it must beat
pages.part: II. Supply: what Vietnam can make
pages.summary: Vietnam's power and labour are cheap, but in fermentation capital is most of the cost. On indicative numbers, fungal biomass protein made in Vietnam costs USD 4,050 to 14,700 per tonne of protein: more than the commodity plant proteins food makers import, but overlapping egg and dairy proteins, so it fits as a functional food ingredient, not a bulk one. Textured soy is cheap to make; the delivered price of food-grade soy flour decides whether a domestic line beats duty-free Chinese imports.

pages.title: Technology fit: which platforms suit Vietnam
pages.part: II. Supply: what Vietnam can make
pages.summary: We test ten technology families against seven Vietnamese conditions: feedstock, industrial base, science readiness, route to market, buyers, competition and capital intensity. Textured plant protein for food fits now. Local legume and rice proteins and fungal foods are worth proving. Precision fermentation fits only as high-value, low-dose ingredients made under contract. Cultivated meat and seafood are research topics for this decade. Feed uses stay in the matrix as a record but are context only, and insects are a benchmark, not a recommendation.

pages.title: What Vietnam eats and pays for protein
pages.part: III. Demand: who would buy it
pages.summary: Vietnamese adults eat enough protein and far more meat than national guidance advises, and eggs and chicken are cheap protein. Tofu and soy milk, the plant protein people already eat, rest almost wholly on imported soybeans. Imported plant-based analogues cost 12 to 18 times as much per gram of protein, so any new protein faces clear targets on price, protein content and format.

pages.title: The incumbent: chay, tofu and soy milk
pages.part: III. Demand: who would buy it
pages.summary: Chay, vegetarian eating on lunar days and festivals, is Vietnam's largest plant-protein occasion, and we estimate that existing chay days already avoid about 25,000 t of meat protein a year. It is the cheapest place to launch a higher-protein ingredient, but the wrong place to count meat displacement.

pages.title: Consumers and new proteins: what people say and what they buy
pages.part: III. Demand: who would buy it
pages.summary: Vietnamese survey respondents are open to plant-based meat, yet only 15% intend to eat less meat and only 3% eat it weekly. Imported analogues cost 12 to 18 times chicken or eggs per gram of protein. Plant milk is the one modern plant category that sells at scale, and people want more protein choice in familiar dishes, not a meat replacement.

pages.title: Fermentation, cultivated meat and blends: demand for the frontier categories
pages.part: III. Demand: who would buy it
pages.summary: Vietnam has no tested or revealed consumer evidence for cultivated meat or precision-fermented foods, only stated attitudes from young or online samples. Blending into foods people already buy is the most likely entry route. But a new fungal or fermented extender has to beat hydrated soy, not lean meat, and avoid being seen as filler.

pages.title: Where protein is bought and eaten: retail, foodservice and institutions
pages.part: III. Demand: who would buy it
pages.summary: Most food is still sold in traditional markets and small grocers (83% of food retail), so a new chilled or frozen protein fits the frozen vegetarian aisle, retailer own brands or kitchens. In factory canteens, where price decides, only an ingredient cheaper than tofu and dry soy-gluten pieces fits; schools are the wrong place to start with a branded meat replacement.

pages.title: Business buyers: the market for protein ingredients
pages.part: III. Demand: who would buy it
pages.summary: Food firms give the clearest evidence of demand for new protein in Vietnam: they imported about USD 285 million of protein ingredients in 2023, and domestic makers have no tariff shelter. A new ingredient has to match the landed cost of Chinese commodity grades, match hydrated soy as a meat extender, or compete with egg and dairy proteins on function.

pages.title: Export demand: who abroad would buy Vietnamese alternative protein
pages.part: III. Demand: who would buy it
pages.summary: Vietnam exports almost no protein ingredients, but it exported USD 128.2 million of dumplings and other stuffed pasta in 2023. Its tariff edge abroad comes with conditions, and retail demand for finished plant-based meat is falling in the United States and flat in Europe.

pages.title: How much demand? Seven routes to 2050
pages.part: III. Demand: who would buy it
pages.summary: Instead of a market-size number, we size seven routes by which domestic or novel protein could reach buyers, in three labelled scenarios. On a benchmark path they create demand for about 19,000 t of protein a year by 2035, mostly by replacing imported ingredients, but displace only about 2,350 t of meat protein (0.2%).

pages.title: Outlook to 2035
pages.part: IV. Futures: 2035 and 2050
pages.summary: Almost every rule change that matters for new protein foods in Vietnam lands in 2025 to 2027, so the direction of the next decade will be visible within about 18 months. We sketch three plausible states for 2035 (import price-taker, feed-first domestic build-out, regulated regional hub), say what each would mean for the protein people eat, and give the signposts that would show which is unfolding. These are scenarios, not forecasts.

pages.title: Drivers to 2050: what is near-certain, what is not
pages.part: IV. Futures: 2035 and 2050
pages.summary: Some forces acting on the protein Vietnamese people eat to 2050 are close to certain: an ageing workforce, fewer smallholder livestock farms, endemic pig disease increasingly from strains the licensed vaccines do not cover, fewer wild fish, tight agricultural emission caps, a sinking and saltier Mekong Delta, and continued dependence on imported soy and maize for the feed behind meat. Others are open. Two external uncertainties matter most for protein made in Vietnam for people: whether imported protein, mostly the feed behind domestic meat, comes under chronic stress, and whether Asia's fermentation industry stays an open market or falls under Chinese price dominance. They become the axes of the 2050 scenarios in chapter 23.

pages.title: Frontier technology: which windows open for Vietnam, and when
pages.part: IV. Futures: 2035 and 2050
pages.summary: The frontier technologies that could reshape protein supply by 2050 all work in the laboratory, but none has yet shown the cost fall that solar power did. Against the food protein ingredients Vietnam already buys, fermentation protein made in Vietnam competes first with egg and dairy proteins, not with cheap plant proteins. For protein for people the windows open in sequence: imported, approved novel ingredients from about 2028 if a new-food route exists, contract precision fermentation and food mycoprotein in 2030 to 2035, and protein from power made in Vietnam not before the 2040s.

pages.title: The protein balance to 2050: what people will eat, and the imports behind it
pages.part: IV. Futures: 2035 and 2050
pages.summary: On trend, the meat protein Vietnamese people eat rises from about 1.01 Mt in 2025 to about 1.45 Mt in 2050 (our model). The share of it resting on imports, directly or through feed, rises from 70% to 78% to about 79% to 87%, and the imported soybean meal behind it from 7.2 Mt to about 10.4 Mt. Replacing meat protein in diets saves the most imports per tonne, but a plant food made from imported soy stays import-dependent, and at the scale demand supports, new protein adds a second source rather than replacing meat.

pages.title: Four worlds in 2050: scenarios for Vietnam's protein supply
pages.part: IV. Futures: 2035 and 2050
pages.summary: We cross two uncertainties, stress on imported protein and whether Asia's fermentation market stays open or falls under Chinese price dominance, to build four scenarios for 2050, not forecasts. Two public goods pay off in every world, five of the seven plays hold in every world with conditions, and high-value precision fermentation is a bet that needs signposts; where Chinese prices dominate, only protein made from domestic inputs adds security.

pages.title: Vietnam 2050: a vision for a measured, more diverse and more secure protein supply
pages.part: IV. Futures: 2035 and 2050
pages.summary: A vision for discussion, not a forecast: by 2050 Vietnam measures the protein its people eat, makes more of it at home and adds new sources beside meat. New routes would supply about 67,000 to 172,000 t of protein a year, about 59,000 to 147,000 t of it made in Vietnam, with milestones tied to the five-year plans from 2026 to 2050.

pages.title: What demand asks of the frontier: product targets, plays and public goods
pages.part: V. What to do
pages.summary: Demand in Vietnam pulls new protein as an ingredient inside foods people already eat, sold to the firms and kitchens that make them, and soy, not meat, is the price an extender must beat. We turn this into ten active target product profiles (TPP-01 to TPP-10), a demand check of the seven active plays and twenty cheap moves, each with a funder or budget.

pages.title: Seven plays and four public goods
pages.part: V. What to do
pages.summary: We describe seven concrete plays for making protein for people in Vietnam, each with the tests that would kill it, and score them on seven criteria with weights readers can change. Domestic textured plant protein, a cassava-starch-to-fermentation-sugar hub and shared pilot and tolling fermentation lead, and four public goods would lower the cost of every play.

pages.title: Policy options
pages.part: V. What to do
pages.summary: Most of what would help Vietnam make protein for people is cheap: a short new-food clause in the Food Safety Law before the vote considered in May 2027, a joint note on precision-fermented proteins and a proportionate novel-food procedure in the law's decree. We rank 19 current options by impact, effort and timing; the expensive ones are shared pilot fermentation and testing capacity.

pages.title: Moves that pay off in any 2050
pages.part: V. What to do
pages.summary: We tested 21 candidate moves against four possible worlds in 2050. Seven no-regret moves pay off in all of them, such as a national protein balance, a new-food route with deadlines and shared food-grade pilot capacity. Most are public and cheap and can start in 2026 to 2028, while two bets should wait for named signposts.

pages.title: What frontier actors asked, and what the answers changed
pages.part: V. What to do
pages.summary: We checked the demand chapters against 80 named actors, from funders to food makers and regulators. Follow-up research changed how to act: schools fill plant-protein days with tofu, and only four of the original nineteen demand moves have a funder that fits and accepts Vietnam. The core conclusion stands: demand pulls new protein as an ingredient sold to the firms that already make food.

pages.title: What we do not know, and who can tell us
pages.part: V. What to do
pages.summary: Desk research has reached diminishing returns. The eighteen unknowns that matter most for protein for people can mostly be closed by a letter to a ministry, a phone call to a starch factory or food maker, or a query to customs. Four of them decide how far the food-security case reaches. We list them in priority order, with the play or move each one unblocks and who to ask. The full register holds 473 open questions and 372 recorded disagreements between sources.

pages.title: Brief for investors
pages.summary: For venture capital, impact investors, private equity and development finance. The study is about protein for people; feed is context only. The near-term theses are business-to-business food ingredients and fermentation services, and most are not venture-shaped. Domestic textured plant protein is an import-substitution plant financed with debt; a cassava-sugar hub and shared pilot fermentation need strategic partners. Underwrite capital cost, input prices and rule risk, price against Chinese imports, and plan for trade-sale exits. The food-security case is real but narrow and favours plays on domestic inputs.

pages.title: Brief for policy makers
pages.summary: For ministries, the National Assembly and provinces. The study is about protein for people; feed is context only. The case is the security of the protein people eat, industrial value and trade. The first security move is a national protein balance, because the food-security resolution has no import or protein indicator. The cheapest high-value step is a new-food clause in the Food Safety Law before passage is considered in May 2027. Most label rules already exist and need enforcing, and the largest gap public money can fill is shared pilot and testing capacity.

pages.title: Brief for startups and founders
pages.summary: The study is about protein for people; feed is context only. Founders should start where the legal route for food is already clear, with familiar plant foods or koji, and aim first to supply food makers rather than launch their own analogue brand. Domestic textured protein is a debt-financed plant to build with a vegetarian food maker or distributor, not alone on venture money. If food security is part of the pitch, prefer domestic inputs.

pages.title: Brief for food manufacturers
pages.summary: Food and beverage companies run on mostly imported protein. They are the natural owners of a domestic textured-protein line and the first customer every play needs. Near-term options are to pool orders behind such a line, test new extenders against the soy already in use, and design plant milks at or below 5 g sugar. Imported frozen pork, cheaper than domestic lean, is the only meat import blends could plausibly displace. Feed appears only as context.

pages.title: Brief for universities and research institutes
pages.summary: The study is about protein for people; feed is context only. Vietnam's research strengths, in fish and shrimp feeding trials, yeast protein expression, stem-cell culture, koji genetics and microalgae, sit next to food protein rather than inside it. The most useful work pairs a Vietnamese raw material or species with a missing food study, such as protein quality, phytate and zinc, strain safety, sensory tests or duckweed food safety. The binding constraint is shared pilot fermentation, food extrusion and protein-quality testing. For food security, the missing data are the domestic share of soybeans in tofu and soy milk, the input origin of new protein foods, a Vietnamese food balance and a swine fever vaccine for the new strains.

pages.title: Brief for international organisations and development finance
pages.summary: For development agencies, foundations, NGOs and foreign governments. The study is about protein for people; feed is context only. Vietnam's capacity to make more protein for people at home is held back by missing public goods: a national protein balance, a novel-food procedure, shared pilot fermentation and protein-quality testing. These fit technical assistance, research grants and first-loss development finance. The evidence does not support funding alternative protein as pandemic prevention. On the demand side, only 4 of the original 19 demand moves have a funder that fits and accepts Vietnam.

pages.title: M1. Method, evidence rules and limits
pages.summary: The study's scope (protein for people first, feed only as context) and how it was designed around six audiences: the first two research waves and the retail audit, the tools used, how evidence was labelled and checked, how earlier drafts were used, and the limits. Sections M1.10 to M1.13 summarise the later rounds, described in full in Appendices M2 to M4.

pages.title: M2. Futures method: how the 2050 chapters were built
pages.summary: How the futures round behind Part IV was designed, researched and checked: the ten questions it answers, the twelve research streams and their 469 sources, the foresight badges on every forward-looking claim, the two-axis scenario method, the stress test of plays and moves, the vision and backcasting method, and the limits of the work. It also marks the feed plays, moves and vision indicators that are no longer recommended now that the study concentrates on protein for people.

pages.title: M3. Demand method: how Part III was built
pages.summary: How the demand round behind Part III was scoped, researched and checked: the questions it answers, eight research streams and their 451 sources, the re-read of the retail audit, the demand evidence tag that separates stated, revealed, tested and inferred evidence, survey quality grades, the demand sizing model, the claims we rejected and the limits of the work.

pages.title: M4. The actor check and expansion waves 7 to 9
pages.summary: How v0.4 was built: an actor check of Part III against 80 named actors and 118 decision questions, then sixteen research lines in three waves, each chosen to ask a different kind of question, with the yield of each line, the rule we used to stop, the decisions taken when folding the results into the report, the contacts that the remaining questions need, and the limits of the work.

pages.title: M5. Changelog and corrections
pages.summary: Every version of this draft report and what it changed, including the refocus on protein for people and the food-security research of v0.8, the citation check of v0.7 and where each page moved in the v0.6 restructure. It lists every correction to earlier drafts, with what it was, what the report now uses, the source and where it appears.

pages.title: S1. Company and actor directory
pages.summary: A guided tour of the 97 companies and organisations in companies.csv, grouped by what they do, with location, scale signal, status and sources, followed by a dated timeline of Vietnamese alternative protein from 2015 to September 2026. Feed firms are kept as context.

pages.title: S2. Retail formulation audit (Nha Trang and Ho Chi Minh City, September 2026)
pages.summary: What 186 plant-protein products on 11 Vietnamese shelves are made of, who makes them and where their protein comes from. Most of the shelf is low in protein, every protein-dense local product runs on imported soy protein or wheat gluten, and no Vietnamese textured soy protein plant was found.

pages.title: S3. Regional comparators and approvals
pages.summary: How Vietnam compares with Singapore, Thailand, Korea, China and other neighbours on novel-food rules, approvals, strategies, open pilot plants and trade, with the full GFI APAC x Hawkwood 'Where to Build' scores and our critique of them.

pages.title: S4. Feedstock data sheets
pages.summary: One data sheet for each Vietnamese raw material and side stream that a process making protein for people could use: volume and how we got it, location, users, prices, composition, seasonality, competing uses, what it could become and what is still unknown. Feed uses appear as context.

pages.title: S5. Industrial facilities and capacity
pages.summary: Vietnam's fermentation, soy, food-processing and starch plants, with feed mills as context: published capacities, a modelled estimate of installed fermentation volume, the 2025 to 2026 feed-industry consolidation, and what we could not find (contract fermentation, protein isolates, food-grade extrusion).

pages.title: S6. Feed and aquafeed market
pages.summary: Context, not a target: the feed market behind the meat, eggs and farmed fish people in Vietnam eat, with feed output and imports, aquafeed by species, fishmeal prices to August 2026 and what Vietnamese mills paid for fishmeal. It also keeps the record of the earlier feed assessment (the displaceable fishmeal pool, incumbent substitutes, trial evidence, buyer economics and the ASC feed-mill register, the prices to beat, the Chinese import counterfactual, and imported inactive yeast, about 9,200 t in 2025 for food and feed, 95% of it at about USD 1.1 per kg), which no longer supports a recommended play.

pages.title: S7. Research landscape and bibliometrics
pages.summary: How much alternative-protein research Vietnam publishes, topic by topic and against its neighbours, which groups and institutions hold the relevant skills, who funds them, and the 11 research gaps Vietnam is well placed to fill.

pages.title: S8. Pilot facilities, laboratories and talent
pages.summary: Where a founder in Vietnam can pilot, test, find land with incentives, hire graduates and buy equipment in 2026. We found no public food-grade pilot fermentation service and no digestibility testing service, and only one laboratory lists amino-acid analysis equipment. The state feed-trial centres, reorganised in 2025 and 2026, are kept as context.

pages.title: S9. Regulatory register and routes to market
pages.summary: The legal routes a new protein food can take in Vietnam as of 23 September 2026, with the feed and aquafeed rules kept as context and as the record. It covers who owns what after the 2025 restructuring, food and GMO rules, incentives, sandboxes, tariffs, a route-to-market table, foreign precedents and the first 25 policy options. It includes the Food Safety Law timetable (two readings, vote considered in May 2027), 0% preferential tariffs on Chinese and ASEAN protein ingredients, and the 2026 label and claim instruments. This is not legal advice.

pages.title: S10. Administrative map after the 2025 reforms
pages.summary: The 34 provincial-level units that replaced Vietnam's 63 on 1 July 2025, where the alternative-protein clusters now sit, the end of the district tier, the 2025 ministry mergers, and practical rules for reading older statistics and addresses.

pages.title: S11. Capital: deals, investors and funding programmes
pages.summary: Every disclosed alternative-protein and adjacent agrifood deal linked to Vietnam, the size of Vietnamese venture and private equity markets, the Entobel insect-feed financing as a deal template, global and regional investment trends, development finance, the new state venture funds, grants open in 2026, accelerators and exit routes.

pages.title: S12. Cost inputs and techno-economic benchmarks
pages.summary: What it costs to make protein in Vietnam: power, water, heat, labour, land, taxes and commodity prices as of 2026, retail protein prices per 100 g of protein, verified techno-economic benchmarks, a tropical cooling estimate, and two indicative cost stacks with every line's basis: textured soy protein, and fungal biomass protein (built as a feed ingredient and kept as the record). The textured-soy stack is built on listed Chinese equipment (USD 761 to 1,573 per t) and adds preferential tariffs: Chinese and ASEAN protein ingredients enter duty-free.

pages.title: S13. State of the science by technology family
pages.summary: What the peer-reviewed evidence says in 2026 about each alternative-protein technology family, from plant proteins and fermentation to duckweed and cultivated seafood, with the main numbers and DOIs, what each means for Vietnam, and a table of corrections to earlier claims. Feed trials are kept as context.

pages.title: D1. Protein diet, chay and price data
pages.summary: The data behind chapters 11 and 12. It covers protein supply and intake by food group; household use of meat, fish, eggs and tofu by area, income and region; food spending and eating out; retail prices per 100 g of protein; demand drivers and projections to 2035; and the protein ladder of Vietnam and its neighbours. It also holds the chay practice and market registers, national diet surveillance (7.9% of adults had a flesh-free day in 2021; 40% ate tofu, soy milk or beans) and what children's school plates carry, including upland boarding schools.

pages.title: D2. Consumer and acceptance evidence register
pages.summary: Every consumer study we found with Vietnamese data on plant-based foods, meat reduction or new proteins, graded for quality. It also holds willingness-to-pay evidence, brand launches and exits, and acceptance records for cultivated meat, fermentation and blends. Of 24 regional firms since 2019, 7 are active. We found no confirmed case of meat in a Vietnamese vegetarian (chay) product from 2015 to 2026.

pages.title: D3. The retail audit re-read for demand
pages.summary: What the September 2026 audit of 186 products in 11 stores says about demand: prices, the cost of a serving of protein, the range on the shelf and label claims. Mass stores carry almost no imported products. Twenty grams of protein from a vegetarian (chay) wrapper costs more than a whole street meal, and no chay food carries a protein claim.

pages.title: D4. Channels and institutions data
pages.summary: The data behind chapter 15 on where people buy and eat protein. It covers food retail by channel and the store counts of every major chain, private label, fresh meat and cold chain, foodservice size and chain outlets, the meat-free items chains and business-to-business platforms have tried, corporate commitments, factory canteens and their dish mix, public meal rules and who writes the menus, the school menu audit, upland boarding meals, hospitals and the army, kitchen protein prices, e-commerce counters, tourism arrivals by market and in Khanh Hoa, and the channel ranking for five product types.

pages.title: D5. Business buyers of protein ingredients
pages.summary: The data behind chapter 16 on the firms that buy protein ingredients for food. It covers Vietnam's imports of 13 protein-ingredient customs lines from 2019 to 2025, as reported by Vietnam and by its trading partners; border and landed prices per kg and per kg of protein; preferential import duties, which are 0% for Chinese, ASEAN and Korean protein ingredients; the monthly timing of Chinese shipments; a map of 27 named buyers and intermediaries with the proteins they use and their likely first novel ingredient; the segment ranking; and the label audit of 118 Vissan products.

pages.title: D6. Export markets and market access
pages.summary: The data behind chapter 17 on who abroad would buy alternative protein made in Vietnam. It covers Vietnam's export lines relevant to alternative protein, with values and markets, including USD 128.2 million of stuffed pasta; demand for plant-based and alternative protein in destination markets from 2022 to 2025; European retailers' plant-protein targets and supplier requirements; mirror trade in wrapped foods and textured protein; the tariffs, label rules and novel-food rules that decide what can be exported; the rules of origin, verified for the EU, that set the recipe conditions on Vietnam's tariff edge; and, as context, feed standards and the trade in inactive yeast.

pages.title: D7. Global and Asian demand benchmarks
pages.summary: What happened to demand for alternative protein where it was tried first: adoption and household penetration in the United States, Europe and Asia; price elasticities and price-parity experiments; price gaps against meat; the effects of institutional and nudge interventions, now including Asian public-meal and corporate-menu precedents and what diet-change programmes deliver per meal and per dollar; displacement of meat and dairy, including restaurant evidence of no displacement; and the track record of long-range market forecasts. These anchor the demand model and the scenario labels of Part III.

pages.title: D8. The demand sizing model
pages.summary: How the model behind the demand-sizing chapter works: seven routes, every assumption with its basis, results for 2025 to 2050, a sensitivity test and conversion into animals spared and CO2e avoided. About 11,000 to 17,000 t of the 19,000 t of protein on the benchmark path in 2035 would be made in Vietnam, and all results are what-if estimates.

pages.title: F1. Milestones and outlook data
pages.summary: The dated calendar of laws, targets and events from 2025 to 2035, and the outlook numbers behind the 2030 and 2035 view: population, meat and feed targets, power and commodity prices, with feed prices as context. It also holds the three 2035 scenarios and a tracker of signposts with sources and thresholds.

pages.title: F2. Drivers, shocks, signals and wildcards to 2050
pages.summary: The evidence behind chapters 20 and 23: the drivers to 2050 (trade, disease, energy, population and climate) and what they mean for the protein people eat, the choice of the two scenario axes, the 16 signposts with their September 2026 status, and full registers of 43 signals, 26 wildcards, 22 external forecasts and 20 past shocks.

pages.title: F3. Frontier technology: evidence, costs and windows
pages.summary: The evidence and calculations behind chapter 21: an evidence card for each of eleven frontier routes, the cost arithmetic for protein made from power in Vietnam, learning rates, carbon costs, AI, approvals, capital, research and the windows table. Every Vietnamese cost and window is our estimate from stated inputs, not a forecast. Comparisons with feed prices are context.

pages.title: F4. The protein and feed balance model
pages.summary: The documentation behind chapter 22: the model that links population and the meat people eat to production, feed and the imported soybean meal and maize behind it. It gives the published projections used, the steps and parameters, four scenarios, full results, a sensitivity test, sanity checks and how to rerun the model. Every value for 2030 to 2050 is our estimate from stated assumptions, not a forecast.

pages.title: F5. Targets, benchmarks and places: the policy and spatial frame to 2050
pages.summary: The evidence behind chapters 24 and 28: every official Vietnamese target relevant to protein supply from 2025 to 2050 and what the targets leave out, how protein and bioeconomy strategies abroad have fared, the map layers and six candidate hubs (clusters of plants on one site), and the full registers of the 25 vision milestones and the 21 moves tested for chapter 28.

pages.title: F6. Aquafeed, marine ingredients and carbon feedstocks to 2050
pages.summary: Context and the record of the earlier feed assessment: fisheries targets, three aquaculture paths to 2050, trash fish, fishmeal and omega-3 for aquafeed, protein crops and climate. Part 2 asks whether residues, side streams and one-carbon feedstocks could supply the 1.32 Mt of glucose the stretch scenario needs in 2050; that part also bears on food fermentation. All 2040 and 2050 values are our what-if estimates, not forecasts.

pages.title: R1. Open questions register
pages.summary: All 473 open questions left by the research, grouped by topic, with why each matters, the cheapest way to close it, who to ask, and its status. The eighteen priorities are ranked in chapter 30.

pages.title: R2. Disagreements log
pages.summary: All 373 cases where sources disagree, with both claims and the position this report takes. We never average disagreeing numbers.

pages.title: R3. Glossary (English and Vietnamese)
pages.summary: 236 terms used in the report, in English and Vietnamese, with short definitions in both languages, grouped by theme, with sections for futures and foresight, the demand side, the actor check and newcomers. Thuật ngữ song ngữ Anh - Việt dùng trong báo cáo.

pages.title: R4. Sources
pages.summary: All 2,480 sources behind the report (806 in v0.1, 469 added by the futures round of v0.2, 451 by the demand round of v0.3, 577 by the actor check and expansion waves of v0.4, 81 by the prologue research of v0.5 and 96 by the food-security round of v0.8, including six from its editorial checks), grouped by the research stream that found them. Each citation code in the text links here and to sources.csv.
